content: Tektins are cytoskeletal proteins that serve as structural components of the outer doublet microtubules found in cilia and flagella. They are also present in centrioles and basal bodies. These proteins are polymeric in nature and assemble into filamentous structures. Tektin filaments have a diameter of approximately 2 to 3 nanometers and are composed of two alpha-helical segments. They exhibit a conserved amino acid sequence, specifically RPNVELCRD. There are different types of tektins, designated as A (53 kDa), B (51 kDa), and C (47 kDa), which can form dimers, trimers, and oligomers in various combinations. These tektins are also associated with tubulin within the microtubule structure. Tektins A and B form heteropolymeric protofilaments, while tektin C forms homodimers. The filaments exist in a supercoiled state, and their structural characteristics suggest an evolutionary relationship to intermediate filaments. As integral components of microtubules, tektins are essential for maintaining the structural integrity of these cellular elements. Mutations in tektin-related genes, such as tektin-t, can result in defects in flagellar function. For example, such mutations may lead to immotility of sperm, which can cause male infertility. Tektins are also believed to play a role in the assembly of basal bodies. The study of tektins has proven valuable in phylogenetic research, as it helps establish evolutionary relationships between organisms. The amino acid sequences of tektins are highly conserved, with significant similarity observed between mouse and human homologs.
